planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter jasmine tolerates poor soil and looks best cascading over a wall or bank where its arching stems can drape freely.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter jasmine tolerates poor soil and looks best cascading over a wall or bank where its arching stems can drape freely. Bright yellow, star-shaped flowers open along bare, arching green stems from late winter into early spring, well ahead of most other flowering shrubs, providing a welcome flush of cheerful color during the last cold weeks of winter dormancy despite lacking the fragrance of its jasmine relatives. Its long, sprawling, cascading stems root wherever they touch soil, making it a useful, tough groundcover for a bank or the top of a retaining wall where its arching branches can spill downward and its winter bloom can be appreciated from below. Prune immediately after flowering to shape and control spread, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and it tolerates hard renewal pruning if the planting becomes overgrown.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11.

directions: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Fully double, camellia-like white flowers open in clusters from summer through fall, releasing the classic, powerfully sweet Arabian jasmine fragrance used to scent jasmine tea, with far more petals per flower than the simpler single or semi-double forms of the species, making this one of the most ornamentally prized jasmine cultivars for fragrance gardens. Its warmth-loving nature makes it a superb container plant that can be moved to a sheltered spot or brought indoors for winter outside the warmest zones, continuing to bloom under bright indoor light with adequate humidity. Water regularly, feed during the growing season to sustain the heavy, fragrant bloom, and prune after flowering to shape and encourage bushier growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; primrose jasmine is semi-evergreen in mild climates and cascades attractively over a wall or bank.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; primrose jasmine is semi-evergreen in mild climates and cascades attractively over a wall or bank. Bright, semi-double, pale yellow flowers resembling small primroses open along arching green stems in late winter and early spring, larger and showier than the flowers of winter jasmine though sharing that relative's lack of fragrance and cascading, wall-draping growth habit. Its glossy, semi-evergreen foliage and long, arching canes make it a good choice for softening a retaining wall, bank, or trellis in mild-winter climates, providing an early, cheerful splash of yellow color when little else is blooming. Prune immediately after flowering to control size and shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and it tolerates hard pruning to rejuvenate an overgrown planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; fountain butterfly bush blooms on old wood in late spring, unlike the more common Buddleja davidii, so prune immediately after flowering rather than in late winter.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; fountain butterfly bush blooms on old wood in late spring, unlike the more common Buddleja davidii, so prune immediately after flowering rather than in late winter. Long, slender, weeping branches are lined with clusters of small, fragrant, lilac-purple flowers in late spring, forming a graceful, fountain-like silhouette quite different from the more upright, spiky growth of the familiar summer-blooming Buddleja davidii, and drawing butterflies in similarly large numbers. Its early bloom time and weeping habit make it a distinctive alternative to the more commonly planted summer butterfly bush, providing a different silhouette and bloom season in a mixed shrub border. Prune immediately after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood unlike davidii-type butterfly bush, and avoid the harder late-winter pruning appropriate for davidii types, which would remove this species' flower buds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter honeysuckle blooms on bare branches in late winter, filling the garden with fragrance well before spring.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter honeysuckle blooms on bare branches in late winter, filling the garden with fragrance well before spring. Small, creamy white, unassuming flowers open along the bare branches in late winter to very early spring, easy to overlook visually but releasing an intense, sweet, lemon-and-jasmine-like fragrance that carries a remarkable distance on a still winter day, making this shrub prized for scent rather than showy bloom. A large, rounded, semi-evergreen to deciduous shrub, it is best sited near a door, window, or path where its understated but powerful winter fragrance can be enjoyed up close during the coldest, least colorful part of the year. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, and note that it has naturalized and become weedy in some regions, so monitor for unwanted seedlings and consider a well-behaved native alternative where invasive spread is a local concern.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Daybreak's Flame loropetalum holds its intense burgundy foliage color best in full sun.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Daybreak's Flame loropetalum holds its intense burgundy foliage color best in full sun. Deep, rich burgundy-purple foliage provides season-long color contrast in a shrub border, punctuated by a heavy flush of vivid magenta-pink, fringed, spidery flowers in spring with lighter repeat bloom through the growing season, a bold, reliable color combination that has made loropetalum a mainstay of Southern landscaping. Its vigorous, adaptable growth and strong dark foliage color make it a versatile choice for a hedge, foundation planting, or specimen shrub, tolerating heat, humidity, and a range of soil conditions across the Gulf South and greater Southeast. Prune after the main spring flush to shape, and provide full sun for the darkest, most saturated foliage color, since shade causes the leaves to green up and lose intensity.
